h1: The 8 Best USB-C to Ethernet Adapters for Laptops, Consoles and Tablets, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best USB-C to Ethernet Adapters: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 USB-C to Ethernet adapters compared on 1Gbps and 2.5G speed, driver support, build, warranty and console compatibility.
summary: The UGREEN 2.5G adapter is the one to buy if your router or switch has a 2.5G port, since it falls back to gigabit without fuss. For a plain gigabit network the Anker is the dependable pick, the TP-Link UE300C is the best for Linux users, and the Belkin carries the longest listed warranty at two years.
intro: Most people think the weak point of a wired connection is the adapter. The real bottleneck is usually the port behind it. A fast adapter plugged into a USB-C port that only runs at slower speeds, or into a router that tops out at gigabit, will never exceed what the slowest link allows.

So this ranking separates speed class first, then looks at driver support, build and warranty. We reviewed eight adapters from their listings and published specs, covering speed rating, operating system support, housing material and warranty length. All eight sit in the budget end of the market, and we say where a listing gives few details.

products.name: UGREEN USB-C to Ethernet Adapter 2.5G
products.verdict: A 2.5Gb adapter on an RTL8156BG chip that still works on gigabit networks.
products.description:
This UGREEN adapter delivers 2.5Gb Ethernet using an RTL8156BG chip, in an aluminum housing with status LEDs, priced $25 to $50. It is backward compatible with 1Gb networks, so it costs you nothing on an older router.

It ranks first because it is the only adapter here that goes beyond gigabit. If your router, switch or home internet plan supports 2.5G, the extra headroom is useful for file transfers and fast fibre plans. The aluminum housing helps spread heat, which matters for a chip that runs warm under load. It costs more than the 1Gbps models and offers no advantage if your network tops out at gigabit.

Buy it if you have a 2.5G port or plan to upgrade. Skip it if your whole network is gigabit and you want the cheapest option.
products.idealFor: Owners of 2.5G routers, switches or fast fibre plans.
products.skipIf: Your network tops out at gigabit speeds.

products.name: Anker USB-C to Ethernet Adapter
products.verdict: Metal shell, woven cable and a year and a half of cover on a plain gigabit adapter.
products.description:
The Anker runs 1Gbps over USB-C 3.0. Its metal shell and woven nylon lead come with 18 months of cover, and it costs under $25. It is a no-surprises gigabit adapter from a familiar accessory brand.

It takes second place because the build details are the sort that actually matter on a travel adapter: a braided cable resists kinking, and an aluminum case copes with being tossed in a laptop bag. Gigabit is enough for most home and office networks. It sits behind the UGREEN 2.5G on speed and tied with several others on warranty length, so it wins on balance more than any single standout feature.

Choose it for a reliable everyday adapter. Skip it if you have 2.5G equipment.
cons: Cable is short on a desk setup
products.idealFor: Everyday use on laptops and tablets at gigabit speed.
products.skipIf: Your router or switch offers 2.5G ports.

products.name: TP-Link UE300C USB-C to Ethernet Adapter
products.verdict: A driver-free 1Gbps adapter that lists Linux support and folds flat.
products.description:
The UE300C is a 1Gbps adapter described as driver-free, including on Linux, with a fold-flat plug about 2.8 inches long, priced under $25. The listing also notes that TP-Link has signed the CISA Secure-by-Design pledge.

It ranks third because explicit Linux support is rare in this category, and it matters for anyone running a laptop on Ubuntu or a server on a USB port. The foldable plug makes it pocket-friendly. It sits behind the Anker because the listing says nothing about cable material or warranty length, which would help compare durability.

It suits Linux users and frequent travellers. Skip it if you want a braided cable or a stated warranty.
products.idealFor: Linux users and travellers who want a small adapter.
products.skipIf: You need a stated warranty or braided cable.

products.name: UGREEN USB-C to Ethernet Adapter 1Gbps
products.verdict: A 1Gbps driver-free adapter with LED status light and listed Switch and Steam Deck support.
products.description:
This UGREEN adapter runs at 1Gbps, is driver-free on most operating systems, has an aluminum alloy case and an LED status light, and is listed as compatible with Nintendo Switch and Steam Deck. It is priced under $25.

It ranks fourth because handheld console compatibility is a real selling point for anyone gaming on a wired connection, where a stable link reduces dropouts. The LED helps confirm the cable is live. The tradeoff against the Anker is that the listing offers no warranty detail.

It works for handheld gamers and laptop users. Skip it if you want warranty detail on the listing.
pros: Works with Switch and Steam Deck
products.idealFor: Handheld gamers who want a wired link.
products.skipIf: You want a clearly stated warranty.

products.name: BENFEI USB-C to Ethernet Adapter
products.verdict: A 1Gbps adapter with Thunderbolt 3 and 4 compatibility and an 18-month warranty.
products.description:
The BENFEI is a 1Gbps adapter that is Thunderbolt 3 and 4 compatible, with woven nylon cabling, an aluminum shell and an unconditional 18-month guarantee, priced under $25.

It ranks fifth because it matches the Anker feature for feature and adds a Thunderbolt compatibility note that reassures owners of recent laptops. The word unconditional on the warranty is also a mild plus. It lacks the brand recognition of Anker or Belkin, which affects confidence over the long term.

It suits Thunderbolt laptop owners. Skip it if you prefer a widely known brand.
products.idealFor: Owners of Thunderbolt laptops wanting a cheap adapter.

products.name: Belkin USB-C to Ethernet Adapter
products.verdict: A gigabit adapter that works with Mac and Windows and carries a 2-year warranty.
products.description:
The Belkin offers up to 1000Mbps Gigabit Ethernet with universal Mac and Windows USB-C compatibility and a 2-year warranty, priced under $25. It is a plain adapter from a major accessory brand.

It ranks sixth because the two-year warranty is the longest listed here, but its other details are thin. There is no mention of housing material or cable type, and no console or Linux support. It does the basic job with the reassurance of a well-known maker.

It suits Mac and Windows users who want a brand name and a longer warranty. Skip it if you need Linux or console support.
products.idealFor: Mac and Windows users who value the warranty.
products.skipIf: You need Linux or console compatibility.

products.name: uni USB-C to Ethernet Adapter 1Gbps
products.verdict: A 1Gbps driver-free adapter with a non-slip, port-clearing design.
products.description:
The uni adapter is 1Gbps and driver-free on most operating systems, with a non-slip, port-clearing design and an 18-month warranty, priced under $25. The port-clearing shape keeps it from blocking adjacent ports.

It ranks seventh because the shape helps on crowded laptops, but little else sets it apart. It matches the rest on speed and warranty and offers no console or Linux claims.

It works for laptops with tightly spaced USB-C ports. Skip it if you want a standout feature.
products.skipIf: You want a feature that sets it apart.

products.name: Amazon Basics USB-C to RJ45 Ethernet Adapter
products.verdict: A 10/100/1000M adapter with reversible USB-C and no external power needed.
products.description:
The Amazon Basics adapter supports 10/100/1000M Ethernet through a reversible USB-C connector, needs no external power, and is listed as Nintendo Switch compatible, priced under $25.

It ranks last because it is the plainest option and the listing gives no warranty, build or driver detail. It still does the core job, and the Switch compatibility note is useful.

It suits a cheap spare adapter or a Switch dock. Skip it if you want documented build or warranty information.
products.idealFor: A cheap spare or a Switch setup.
products.skipIf: You want documented build and warranty.

whatMatters.detail: Gigabit adapters match most home networks, while 2.5G adapters need a 2.5G router or switch to use the extra speed. The adapter is only as fast as the slowest link. Check your router and switch port speeds before paying more.
Driver-free adapters work on plug-in, which is convenient. Some chipsets need a driver on older systems. Look for wording about your operating system on the listing, especially for Linux.

The chipset determines compatibility and stability, such as the RTL8156BG in the UGREEN 2.5G. Realtek chips are common and widely supported. Check the listing for the chip name if you run an unusual operating system.
Aluminum cases and braided cables last longer in a bag than thin plastic. A short fixed cable can limit reach. Check the material and the cable length on the listing.

Most adapters work with any USB-C port, but Thunderbolt, handheld consoles and tablets can differ. Look for named compatibility, like the Thunderbolt 3 and 4 note on the BENFEI. Confirm your device is listed.

faq.q: Will it work with my phone or tablet?
faq.a: Often yes, if the device supports USB Ethernet. Check your device's documentation, since some tablets and phones do not recognise adapters. Listings that name tablets or consoles are safer.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when buying one?
faq.a: Paying for 2.5G when the network is gigabit. The extra speed goes unused. Check your router ports first.

faq.q: Is a 2.5G adapter worth it over gigabit?
faq.a: Only if your router or switch has a 2.5G port. The UGREEN also works on gigabit, so it is safe to buy for later. Otherwise a 1Gbps adapter costs less.

faq.q: Do I need to install drivers?
faq.a: Most listed adapters are driver-free on modern systems, including the TP-Link on Linux. Older operating systems may need a driver. Check the listing for your system.
No. The Amazon Basics listing notes that no external power is required, and the others draw power from the USB-C port as well.

faq.q: Why is my connection slower than expected?
faq.a: The USB port, cable or router may limit speed. Try a different port and a good Ethernet cable, and check the link speed in your system settings.

finalTake: Buy the UGREEN 2.5G adapter if your network can use it, and the Anker for a dependable gigabit pick. The TP-Link UE300C is the one for Linux, the UGREEN 1Gbps suits handheld gaming, and the Belkin has the longest warranty. Check your router speed before you spend.
